newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Clinton calls for legal action on greenhouse gases.
newsitem.headline: Clinton calls for legal action on greenhouse gases.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton on Friday called for legally binding commitments to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

"I call upon the community of nations to agree to legally binding commitments to fight climate change," Clinton said in an environment speech in a seaside park on Australia's tropical northeast coast.
"We must stand together against the threat of global warming," said Clinton on the second last day of his five-day visit to Australia.

"A greenhouse may be a good place to raise plants, but it is no place to nurture our children. And we can avoid dangerous global warming if we beging today and if we begin together," he said. "We must work to reduce harmful greenhouse gas emissions."
He said the 1987 Montreal Protocol had slowed production and consumption of chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), the "chemicals which have been eating a hole in the earth's ozone layer".
"We are on our way to closing the ozone hole ... now we must see to it that this landmark treaty is enforced from one corner of the earth to another," Clinton said.

"These gases released by cars and power plants and burning forests ... are literally warming our planet. If they continue unabated the consequences will be nothing short of devastating for the children here in this audience and their children."
Clinton's call for legally binding commitments to reduce greenhouse gases is in contrast to the U.S. stance at the Rio Earth Summit in 1992 when Washington avoided such a stance.
Clinton also called for a reduction in global toxic waste.
"Toxic chemicals and pesticides found here and in the United States can still find their way into our lives, endangering our lives, our lands and our children," Clinton said.
"Let us now forge a global agreement to stop these toxic substances from being released into the world around us."
Clinton also called on the United Nations to develop a strategy for sustainable management of the world's forests, saying that deforestation was clearing an area the size of South Korea annually.
The president said protection of the environment and economic growth were compatable, adding that enviromental destruction contributed to conflict, citing the troubles in drought-striken Africa.

Clinton praised Australia for its efforts in protecting the World Heritage-listed Great Barrier Reef, the world's largest coral reef system consisting of 2,600 reefs linked for 2,500 km (1,550 miles) along the coast. "We share a responsibility to preserve a future for our children and grandchildren, we must care for our shared environment," Clinton said.
"It is a practial and moral imperative," he said.
"We are citizens of not only individual nations but this small and fragile planet. We must be allies in the 21st century to protect the earth's environment."
After the speech, Clinton boated out to the Great Barrier Reef, some 30 nautical miles offshore, to go swimming and snorkelling.
Clinton flies to the Philippines on Saturday for next week's APEC summit.
